title: Always know the smallest
objectives: Use a heap to keep the top $k$ items.
Push and pop on a binary heap stored in a list
Use `heapq` as a min-heap, negating for a max-heap

screens.title: A tree in a list
screens.prose: We must always know the smallest of a stream of prices. This tree keeps every parent no larger than its children. It is stored in a plain list, level by level, left to right.
screens.question: Tap the list cells holding the two children of 5.

hints.text: In the tree, 5 has two children. Find them, then find them in the list.
The tree's third level is 9, 6, 7, 8, stored from index 3.
9 and 6 are 5's children, at indices 3 and 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the tree level by level into the list.

byKey.c2: 3 is 5's sibling: both are children of 2, the root.
byKey.c1: Index 1 holds 5 itself. Its children come later in the list.
byKey.c5: 7 is a child of 3, at index 2. 5's children come just before it.

explain.text: 5 sits at index 1 and its children at 3 and 4. In general the children of index $i$ sit at $2i + 1$ and $2i + 2$, so no links are stored. This is a **binary heap**; the smallest value is always at index 0.

screens.title: Up to the parent
screens.prose: Going down, the children of index $i$ are at $2i + 1$ and $2i + 2$. A new value will need to go up instead.
screens.question: Tap the parent of the 7 at index 5.

hints.text: Which index $i$ has 5 as $2i + 1$ or $2i + 2$?
Index 2, which holds 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the index whose children are 5 and 6.

byKey.c1: Index 1's children are 3 and 4. Index 5 belongs to index 2.
byKey.c4: Index 4 is a sibling level, not a parent. The parent is nearer the front.

explain.text: Index 2 has children $2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5$ and $2 \cdot 2 + 2 = 6$. Undoing that, the parent of $i$ is $(i - 1) // 2$: $(5 - 1) // 2 = 2$, and $(6 - 1) // 2 = 2$ too.

screens.title: Push: sift up
screens.prose: To push 4, append it at the end, index 7. Its parent, 9, is larger, so the rule breaks. Repair it by swapping 4 with its parent while the parent is larger.
screens.question: Restore the heap.

ops.label: Stop here
ops.why: Its parent, 9, is larger than 4, so the rule is still broken. Swap upwards.

ops.label: Stop here
ops.why: Its parent, 5, is still larger than 4. Swap again.

ops.label: Swap 4 with its parent
ops.why: 2 is smaller than 4, so the rule already holds. Swapping would put 4 above 2.

hints.text: Compare 4 with its parent each time: swap only if the parent is larger.
9 > 4, then 5 > 4: two swaps.
Swap, swap, then stop: 2 is smaller than 4.

feedback.correct: Two swaps up, then 2 stops it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep swapping while the parent is larger, and stop as soon as it is not.

explain.text: 4 climbed past 9 and 5 and stopped under 2. Each swap moves one level up, so a push makes at most as many swaps as the tree has levels. This is **sift-up**.

screens.title: Pop: sift down
screens.prose: To pop, take 2 from index 0. Move the last item, 9, into the hole at the top. Now repair downwards: swap 9 with a child while a child is smaller.
screens.question: Restore the heap.

ops.label: Swap with the larger child
ops.why: Then 4 sits above 3, its new child, and the rule breaks there.

ops.label: Stop here
ops.why: 9 is larger than both children, so it cannot stay on top.

ops.label: Swap with the larger child
ops.why: Then 8 sits above 7, and the rule breaks there.

ops.label: Stop here
ops.why: 9 is still larger than its children, 7 and 8.

hints.text: Only the smaller child can safely move up above its sibling.
At the top, the smaller child is 3.
Swap with 3, then with 7, then stop: index 5 has no children.

feedback.correct: 9 sank past 3 and 7, and 3 is the new minimum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap with the smaller child while it is smaller than 9.

explain.text: Swapping with the smaller child keeps that child no larger than its sibling. 9 sank one level per swap. This is **sift-down**, and like sift-up it costs at most the number of levels.

screens.title: How far can it climb
screens.prose: Each swap moves the new value up one level. Level $d$ of a heap holds $2^d$ items, so a heap of $n$ items has $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ levels.

state.caption: A push climbs one path: here 7, 3, 1, 0

screens.question: A heap holds 1,000,000 orders. At most how many swaps does one push make?

hints.text: Find the largest $d$ with $2^d \le 1{,}000{,}000$.
So there are 20 levels, and the climb from the bottom to the top is 19 swaps.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the levels, then the steps between them.

byKey.levels: There are 20 levels, but swaps happen between levels: 19.
byKey.scan: A push never looks at every item, only at one path from the bottom to the top.
byKey.half: Halving the count once is one level. Count how many halvings reach 1.

explain.text: $2^{19} \le 10^6 < 2^{20}$, so the heap has 20 levels and a push climbs at most 19. Pop is the same going down. Both are $O(\log n)$.

screens.title: Push and pop by hand
screens.prose: Write the two operations on a plain list, without `heapq`. `pop` is only called on a non-empty heap. Watch the edge case: popping the last item leaves nothing to move to the top.

hints.text: `push`: append, then swap with the parent at `(i - 1) // 2` while the parent is larger.
`pop`: save `heap[0]`, take the last item off with `heap.pop()`, and if anything is left put it at index 0.
Then sift down: find the smaller of the children at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2` that exist; swap while it is smaller.

feedback.correct: Both operations keep the heap rule after every change.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[1, 3, 8, 5]`. The 1 must climb two levels: keep swapping while the parent is larger.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 pops the only item. After `heap.pop()` the list is empty: do not write to index 0.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 checks the heap after a pop. Swap with the smaller child, not the first one.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 checks for `heapq`. Write the swaps yourself here; the next screens use `heapq`.

explain.text: Both loops walk one path, so both are $O(\log n)$. Moving the last item to the top keeps the list packed, which is what lets index arithmetic replace links.

canvas.caption: The smallest is always at index 0

screens.title: Which end does heapq pop
screens.prose:
We want the three largest trades so far. This code stores each trade negated, and pops whenever the heap holds more than three.

```python
import heapq
h = []
for x in [120, 45, 300, 80, 210, 60]:
    heapq.heappush(h, -x)
    if len(h) > 3:
        heapq.heappop(h)
```
screens.question: Which trades are left in `h`, as positive sizes?

options.why: You read `heappop` as removing the smallest trade. Stored as −300, the largest trade is the smallest value, so it goes first.
Those are the last three to arrive. A heap keeps items by value, not by arrival.

hints.text: `heapq` always pops the smallest stored value.
Which stored value is smallest: −45 or −300?
−300 is smallest, so the largest trades are popped first. The three smallest trades stay.

feedback.correct: The negation turned it into a keeper of the smallest trades.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run it: `heappop` removes the smallest stored number.

byKey.b: You assumed `heapq` pops from the top of a max-heap. It is a min-heap, and negating made the big trades the smallest values.

explain.text: `heapq` is a min-heap: `heappop` removes the smallest stored value. Negated, the largest trade is the smallest value, so it is popped first. To keep the $k$ largest, store them as they are and pop the smallest.

screens.title: What a heap buys
screens.prose:
A heap keeps just enough order to find the smallest:

$$\text{peek: } O(1), \qquad \text{push, pop: } O(\log n), \qquad \text{top } k \text{ of } n\text{: } O(n \log k).$$

Sorting after every update costs $O(n \log n)$ each time. Popping all $n$ items returns them in order: that is **heapsort**, $O(n \log n)$.
screens.question: You want the 10 largest of 1,000,000 trades, using a min-heap of size 10. About how many levels does each new trade climb at most?

options.why: That is a heap of every trade. This one never holds more than 10.
A heap does not scan its items. It walks one path, about 3 levels for 10 items.
Each trade touches only the small heap, not every trade so far.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How big does the heap ever get?

explain.text: The heap never holds more than $k = 10$ items, so each trade costs $O(\log 10)$. Over $n$ trades that is $O(n \log k)$, far less than sorting all of them.

screens.title: Orders by price, then time
screens.prose:
Resting sell orders go in a `heapq` as `(price, time, order_id)` tuples. Tuples compare by their first item, then by the next on a tie.

```python
asks = []
heapq.heappush(asks, (100.03, 1, "A1"))
heapq.heappush(asks, (100.02, 4, "A2"))
heapq.heappush(asks, (100.02, 2, "A3"))
heapq.heappush(asks, (100.05, 3, "A4"))
```
screens.question: Which order is at `asks[0]`?

options.why: A2 ties A3 on price, but arrived later. On a tie the earlier time, 2, wins.
A1 arrived first, but price comes first in the tuple: £100.02 beats £100.03.
A4 has the highest price. A min-heap puts the lowest price on top.

hints.text: The lowest price wins first.
A2 and A3 tie at £100.02. Compare their times.
A3 arrived at time 2, before A2 at time 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare prices first, then times.

explain.text: The lowest price wins, and on a tie the earlier time. Exchanges call this **price-time priority**. Lesson 18 builds an order book on it.

screens.title: The largest trades of the day
screens.prose: A feed streams every trade size of the day, and the desk wants the $k$ largest. Keep a min-heap of at most $k$ sizes: its top is the smallest of the best so far, the one to beat.
screens.question: Write `top_k(xs, k)`: the $k$ largest values of `xs`, largest first, using `heapq` and a heap of at most $k$ items.

hints.text: Push the first $k$ values. After that, a new value only matters if it beats `h[0]`.
`heapq.heapreplace(h, x)` pops the smallest and pushes `x` in one step.
Handle `k <= 0` first. At the end return `sorted(h, reverse=True)`: only $k$ items to sort.

feedback.correct: One pass, a heap of $k$, and $O(n \log k)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[300, 210, 120]`. If you got the smallest three, you negated the values or popped the wrong end.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has `k = 0`: return an empty list before touching the heap.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has repeats: `[7, 7]`. Replace only when a value is strictly larger than `h[0]`, and keep duplicates.

ideas: A binary heap is a tree stored in a list: children of $i$ at $2i + 1$ and $2i + 2$, parent at $(i - 1) // 2$, smallest at index 0.
Push appends and sifts up; pop moves the last item to the top and sifts down, swapping with the smaller child. Both are $O(\log n)$.
For the $k$ largest of a stream, keep a min-heap of size $k$: $O(n \log k)$.

A push is $O(\log n)$, not $O(n)$, and reading `h[0]` is $O(1)$.
